description: a multidisciplinary team founded by a physiotherapy graduate passionate about neuroscience, neurorehabilitation, AI,and space medicine.Our mission is to develop an AI-powered health monitoring system for astronauts,focusing on brain health, cognitive performance, sleep, balance, and motor function during space missions. We welcome passionate members skilled in programming, AI,neuroscience ,medicine,biomedical engineering, data science,UI/UX design. Let's shape the future of space healthcare
summary: is a web platform that helps astronauts and flight surgeons follow how the human body adapts to spaceflight, from the pre-flight baseline through launch and long-duration missions to landing and recovery on Earth. Astronauts complete a short daily check-in covering sleep, heart, brain and balance (with a 20-second reaction game), muscles, breathing, mood, nutrition and symptoms. Each entry travels to Earth through a simulated communication link with realistic Earth-orbit, Moon or Mars delays, so doctors always know what has arrived and how old it is. Astronauts see their trends on a personal dashboard and mission health timeline. Doctors review the data in a console with a prioritised queue, daily reports and weekly reports. Nova, our assistant, answers only from NASA and peer-reviewed sources, shows its references and confidence, and sends urgent symptoms straight to the medical team. The project addresses NASA’s spaceflight hazards by catching changes early and keeping data honest, supporting safer Moon and Mars missions and remote care on Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works
NEUROSPACE 360 is a website with two sides: one for astronauts and one for their flight surgeon on Earth. Every day the astronaut fills in a short check-in, one step per body system: sleep, heart, a 20-second reaction game for the brain, balance, muscles, breathing, mood, food and water, and a body map for symptoms. If they skip a question, we leave it blank. We never guess.

What we cared about most was time. In space, data doesn’t reach the doctor instantly, so every check-in has three timestamps: when it was recorded, when it left the spacecraft and when it reached Earth. You can switch between Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars to see how the delay changes. The doctor’s reply travels back the same way.

The astronaut gets a dashboard with their trends and simple alerts, a mission timeline from before launch to after landing, a brain and balance lab with a holographic brain, and a planetary simulator. The doctor gets a crew overview, a review queue sorted by urgency, daily reports and weekly reports. We also built Nova, a small assistant that only answers from NASA and peer-reviewed sources, shows where each answer comes from and how sure it is, and passes anything that sounds urgent straight to the doctor instead of guessing.

Benefits and impact
Small changes, like a few nights of bad sleep or rising dizziness, can be spotted early instead of after the mission. The doctor saves time because the most important cases come first. On long missions to the Moon or Mars, where help is minutes away, crews need tools like this to look after themselves. We also see real use on Earth: remote rehabilitation, telemedicine in rural areas, and follow-up for patients with balance or neurological problems.

Tools we used
We wrote the site in HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript and host it on GitHub Pages. We used Three.js for the 3D planets, and built the charts ourselves in SVG. Passwords are protected with the browser’s built-in encryption tools (Web Crypto). Nova is a lightweight search engine we wrote ourselves (TF-IDF), not a large AI model. Our content comes from NASA’s Human Research Program, NASA technical reports, the NSSDCA fact sheets and Curiosity’s radiation data, plus the Canadian Space Agency. We used AI tools to help write code and text, Canva for the presentation, and Python for image work and testing.

What makes it creative
Most health dashboards assume data arrives instantly. Ours treats time the way a real mission does: there’s space time, Earth time and the delay in between. We also tried to make learning about the body enjoyable, with the holographic brain, small hands-on demos and a friendly assistant.

What we considered
Safety came first. This is an educational prototype, not a medical device, and it never diagnoses. A human always decides. For privacy, each doctor only sees their own astronauts, and we collect as little as possible. We label every number as measured, self-reported, estimated or simulated, so nobody mistakes demo data for real data. The site also works on phones, with a keyboard and for people who prefer reduced motion.
